paras: The threatened lynching of James Hawks took place in Syracuse, New York, on the afternoon of July 9, 1882, when a crowd pursued Hawks, a laborer accused of stabbing a woman to death, with cries of "Lynch him!" and surrounded the police station where he was held. No attack on the station was reported, and Hawks was convicted of second-degree murder that December and sent to prison for life. Most papers treated the case as a wife murder, and only one widely reprinted dispatch mentioned the crowd.

Hawks, described in one dispatch as "a dissolute laboring man" of about 45 who had been married four times, lived in a neighborhood of Syracuse "commonly known as 'Africa.'" That dispatch called him "a terror to the neighborhood" and said he and the woman had been drinking that day. None of the reports states the race of Hawks, of the woman, or of the crowd.

At about 5 o'clock the woman, reported in July as Mrs. Hawks, was returning along Grape Street with a pail of beer when Hawks, who was intoxicated, stabbed her to the heart with a jackknife. According to the dispatch carried by the Wilmington Daily Gazette, she had stopped to talk with "two colored men," which "so enraged her husband that he rushed out and stabbed her." That account said she died instantly, while the New-York Tribune's version had her run about thirty feet, cling to a tree and die in about fifteen minutes.

The crowd of men, women and children who saw the stabbing followed Hawks for several blocks, shouting "Murderer! Murderer! Lynch him!", while police at first paid little attention, "thinking he was crazy." Hawks was arrested, and when told the woman was dead he reportedly said, "I am glad of it. It is a good thing for me." The police station was then "surrounded by an excited crowd, anxious to lynch the murderer," but no report describes an attempt to seize him.

Hawks, now spelled Hawkes, was tried at Syracuse, and on December 5, 1882, the jury returned a verdict of murder in the second degree. The trial reports named the dead woman as Amelia Hall, "his paramour," or as Amelia Hull, "the woman with whom he had been living for several years," rather than as his wife. A Washington paper reported a few days later that he had been sent to state prison for life. No report of an inquest or of any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

Two separate Syracuse dispatches of July 9 went out over the wires and appeared the next morning from New York to St. Paul and Savannah. The more common version, printed under headlines such as "Wife Murder at Syracuse," "Drunken Uxoricide" and "Unprovoked Wife-Murder," told only of the stabbing, the arrest and Hawks's remark. The other version, headed "Stabbing His Wife to Death," ran in the Wilmington Daily Gazette and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on July 10 and in the Anderson Intelligencer of South Carolina on July 20, where it appeared twice in the same issue.

Shorter notices ran in crime roundups such as the Wilmington Daily Republican's "Sunday's Crimes" and the Huntsville Gazette's "Personal and General" column. No paper commented on the crowd's threat, which the dispatch reported as part of the "great excitement" the murder caused.

The crowd and its lynching cry appear only in the dispatch printed by the Daily Gazette and its reprints; the Tribune's version does not mention a crowd, though it does not deny one. The woman's identity also shifted, from "Mrs. Hawks" in July to Amelia Hall or Hull, his companion of several years, in the December trial reports, which are the later and likely better-informed source.

bases: One wire dispatch reports a crowd chasing James Hawks with cries of 'Lynch him!' and surrounding the police station 'anxious to lynch the murderer', with no attempt on the station reported (A1, A2, A21).
A crowd of men, women and children threatened to lynch Hawks for the stabbing, but he was held by police and later tried and imprisoned, so no one was killed by the crowd (A1, A27, A29).

The killing itself is corroborated by two independent wire versions and the December trial reports, but the crowd pursuit and lynching threat appear in only one dispatch, reprinted (A1, A2, A21), while the other version mentions no crowd (A3, A5).
